skill.title: HTTP
skill.summary: Method semantics, status codes, caching and browser security rules.
skill.description: Know what each part of an HTTP exchange promises: idempotency, status code meaning, what caches may store, and how browsers enforce cross-origin rules.

questions.title: Which method isn't idempotent?
questions.prompt: According to the HTTP specification, which of these methods is not idempotent?

options.text: `GET`
`PUT`
`DELETE`
`POST`

questions.explanation: A method is idempotent when repeating the same request has the same intended effect on the server as sending it once. `GET`, `PUT` and `DELETE` are defined that way; `POST` is not, which is why clients cannot blindly retry it after a timeout.
rubric: Defines idempotency in terms of effect on server state.
Identifies `POST` as not idempotent.
Connects idempotency to whether retries are safe.
misconceptions: Idempotent means the response is identical each time.
`DELETE` is not idempotent because the second call returns 404.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Identifies POST and defines idempotency by its effect on server state.

questions.title: Authenticated but not allowed
questions.prompt: A request carries a valid access token for user Ada, but Ada isn't permitted to delete this project. Which status code fits best?

options.text: `400 Bad Request`
`401 Unauthorized`
`403 Forbidden`
`409 Conflict`

questions.explanation: `401` means the request lacks valid authentication credentials; the server knows who Ada is, so that doesn't apply. `403` means the server understood the request and refuses to authorise it. Some APIs return `404` instead to avoid revealing that the resource exists.
rubric: Distinguishes authentication (401) from authorisation (403).
Chooses 403 for an authenticated but unauthorised request.
Mentions 404 as a deliberate choice to hide resource existence.
misconceptions: 401 is the correct code for any permission failure, because of its name.
Permission errors are client syntax errors (400).
questions.acceptance_criteria: Chooses 403 and distinguishes authentication from authorisation.

questions.title: Before a cross-origin JSON POST
questions.prompt: A page on `https://app.example.com` calls `fetch("https://api.example.com/orders", { method: "POST", headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }, body })`. What does the browser do first?

options.text: Sends the POST, then blocks the response unless the API returns CORS headers
Sends an `OPTIONS` preflight and only sends the POST if the API allows it
Nothing special; both origins share the same registrable domain
Refuses the request, because browsers never allow cross-origin POSTs

questions.explanation: Different subdomains are different origins. `Content-Type: application/json` is not a CORS-safelisted value, so the browser first sends an `OPTIONS` preflight and proceeds only if the response allows the origin, method and headers. CORS is enforced by browsers to protect users; it does not stop non-browser clients calling the API.
rubric: Recognises the two hosts are different origins.
Explains that a JSON content type triggers a preflight.
Describes the preflight's role in allowing the actual request.
States that CORS is browser-enforced and not a server-side access control.
misconceptions: CORS protects the API from all unauthorised clients.
Subdomains of the same site share an origin.
questions.acceptance_criteria: States the browser sends an OPTIONS preflight first because the JSON content type crosses origins.

questions.title: Caching a personalised response
questions.prompt: `GET /me` returns the signed-in user's profile and sits behind a CDN. Which caching headers would you send, and what could go wrong with a careless choice? Then describe how you would cache a public `GET /courses/{id}` that changes a few times a day.
questions.hint: Who may store the response: the browser, the CDN, or both?
questions.explanation: Personalised responses must not be stored by shared caches: send `Cache-Control: private` (or `no-store` for sensitive data). A careless `public` lets the CDN serve one user's profile to another. For public content use `public, max-age` and/or `s-maxage` with validators (`ETag`/`Last-Modified`), and consider `stale-while-revalidate` or purging on change.
rubric: Uses `private` or `no-store` for the personalised response.
Explains the data-leak risk of shared caching.
Uses `max-age`/`s-maxage` for public content.
Adds validation with `ETag` or `Last-Modified`.
Mentions a freshness strategy such as `stale-while-revalidate` or purging.
misconceptions: CDNs never cache responses to authenticated requests.
`no-cache` means do not store.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Uses private or no-store for /me, explains the shared-cache leak risk, and caches the public endpoint with validation.

questions.title: Retry-safe payments
questions.prompt: Mobile clients call `POST /payments`. On flaky networks they time out and retry, and some customers are charged twice. Design an idempotency-key mechanism: what the client sends, what the server stores, how concurrent duplicates are handled, and how long keys are kept.
questions.hint: A timed-out request may or may not have been processed.
questions.explanation: The client generates a unique key per logical operation and resends it on every retry. The server stores the key (scoped to the account) with a fingerprint of the request and the final response, enforced by a unique constraint. A retry with the same key returns the stored response; a key reused with a different body is rejected. Concurrent duplicates are serialised by the unique constraint or a lock, with the second request waiting or receiving a conflict. Keys expire after a window longer than the client's retry horizon.
rubric: Has the client generate one key per logical operation and reuse it on retries.
Stores key, request fingerprint and final response with a uniqueness guarantee.
Returns the stored response for duplicates and rejects mismatched bodies.
Handles concurrent in-flight duplicates explicitly.
Defines a retention window and scopes keys to the account.
misconceptions: Turning off client retries solves duplicate charges.
Checking for a recent identical payment amount is a reliable deduplication method.

resources.title: Stripe engineering: Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency
Patterns of Distributed Systems: Idempotent receiver

questions.acceptance_criteria: Designs client-generated keys stored with a uniqueness guarantee and the stored response, and handles concurrent duplicates.

questions.title: A cross-site form post
questions.prompt: Your session cookie is set with `SameSite=Lax; Secure; HttpOnly`. A malicious site auto-submits a hidden form that POSTs to your app. Is the session cookie sent with that request?
questions.hint: Which kinds of cross-site requests does `Lax` still allow?

options.text: Yes: `Lax` only blocks cookies on cross-site `GET` requests
Yes: `HttpOnly` cookies are always attached to form submissions
No: `Lax` cookies are sent cross-site only on top-level `GET` navigations
No: `Secure` cookies are never sent to forms on other sites

questions.explanation: With `SameSite=Lax` the browser withholds the cookie from cross-site subrequests and from cross-site POSTs, and sends it only on top-level navigations with safe methods such as following a link. That blocks this classic CSRF attack, so state-changing actions must never use GET. `HttpOnly` stops scripts reading the cookie and `Secure` limits it to HTTPS; neither controls cross-site sending.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “No: `Lax` cookies are sent cross-site only on top-level `GET` navigations”. With `SameSite=Lax` the browser withholds the cookie from cross-site subrequests and from cross-site POSTs, and sends it only on top-level navigations with safe methods such as following a link.
rubric: States that the cookie is not sent with the cross-site POST.
Explains that Lax allows only top-level safe-method navigations.
Distinguishes SameSite from HttpOnly and Secure.
Notes that state changes must not use GET.
misconceptions: HttpOnly prevents CSRF.
SameSite=Lax blocks every cross-site request.

questions.title: Two editors, one document
questions.prompt: Clients fetch a document with its `ETag` and send updates with `If-Match: <etag>`. Alice saves first; then Bob saves using the ETag he fetched before Alice's change. What should the server return to Bob?
questions.hint: Which status code is defined for a failed `If-Match` precondition?

options.text: `409 Conflict`, because the document has changed
`412 Precondition Failed`, because `If-Match` no longer matches
`428 Precondition Required`, because the ETag is stale
`304 Not Modified`, because Bob's copy is outdated

questions.explanation: `If-Match` makes the update conditional on the resource still having that ETag. After Alice's save the ETag changed, so the precondition fails and the server must not apply Bob's write: 412 Precondition Failed. 428 is for servers that require a conditional request when the client sent none, and 304 answers conditional GETs. This is optimistic concurrency control over HTTP; the client then refetches and merges or asks the user.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “412 Precondition Failed`, because `If-Match` no longer matches”. `If-Match` makes the update conditional on the resource still having that ETag.
rubric: Chooses 412 Precondition Failed.
Explains that the update is conditional on the ETag.
Distinguishes 428 (missing precondition) and 304 (conditional GET).
Describes what the client does next.
misconceptions: 409 is the standard response for a failed precondition.
ETags are only for caching.

questions.title: French users see English pages
questions.prompt: `GET /products/42` returns English or French text depending on the `Accept-Language` header, with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=300`. Behind a CDN, French users sometimes receive English. What is the correct fix?
questions.hint: What does the CDN use as the cache key by default?

options.text: Send `Cache-Control: private` so only browsers cache the response
Add `Vary: Accept-Language` (or move the language into the URL)
Lower `max-age` to 10 seconds so wrong versions expire quickly
Add an `ETag` so the CDN revalidates every request

questions.explanation: The CDN keys its cache by URL, so whichever language is stored first is served to everyone. `Vary: Accept-Language` tells caches the response depends on that header, so they store variants separately. Because `Accept-Language` has many distinct values, putting the language in the URL (`/fr/products/42`) usually caches far better. `private` gives up shared caching, a short TTL only narrows the window, and an ETag does not separate variants.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “Add `Vary: Accept-Language` (or move the language into the URL)”. The CDN keys its cache by URL, so whichever language is stored first is served to everyone.
rubric: Explains that the cache key ignores the header.
Adds `Vary: Accept-Language` or a language-specific URL.
Notes the fragmentation cost of varying on a high-cardinality header.
Explains why the other options do not fix the mismatch.
misconceptions: Caches automatically account for request headers.
Short TTLs fix incorrect cache sharing.

questions.title: Keeping a response out of caches
questions.prompt: An API returns a user's bank statement. Which `Cache-Control` directive stops browsers and shared caches from storing the response at all?
questions.hint: Which directive is about storage, and which are about reuse?

options.text: `no-cache`
`no-store`
`max-age=0`
`must-revalidate`

questions.explanation: `no-store` tells every cache not to store the response. Despite its name, `no-cache` allows storing but requires revalidation with the origin before each reuse. `max-age=0` makes the response stale immediately, and `must-revalidate` forbids serving it stale; neither forbids storing it.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “no-store”. `no-store` tells every cache not to store the response.
rubric: Chooses `no-store`.
Explains that `no-cache` means revalidate, not do not store.
Distinguishes freshness directives from storage.
misconceptions: `no-cache` means do not cache.
`max-age=0` prevents storage.

questions.title: A conditional GET
questions.prompt: A browser has a cached copy of `/api/catalog` with `ETag: "v42"`. It sends `If-None-Match: "v42"`, and the catalog has not changed. What should the server respond?
questions.hint: What does the browser already have?

options.text: `200 OK` with the full catalog again
`304 Not Modified` with no body
`412 Precondition Failed`
`204 No Content` with the ETag only

questions.explanation: `If-None-Match` asks for the resource only if its current ETag differs. When it matches, the server replies `304 Not Modified` without a body, and the browser reuses its cached copy, saving bandwidth and serialisation. `412` is for failed `If-Match` preconditions on writes; `204` means a successful response with no content, which would not tell the cache to reuse its copy.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “304 Not Modified` with no body”. `If-None-Match` asks for the resource only if its current ETag differs.
rubric: Chooses 304.
Explains that the cached body is reused.
Distinguishes If-None-Match from If-Match and 412.
misconceptions: A matching ETag should return the body again.
412 is used for cache hits.

questions.title: Cookies and a wildcard origin
questions.prompt: A front end at `https://app.example.com` calls `https://api.example.com` with `fetch(url, { credentials: "include" })`. The API responds with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. What does the browser do?
questions.hint: Which value of Access-Control-Allow-Origin is allowed with credentials?

options.text: Sends the cookies and gives the response to the page, since both CORS headers are set
Blocks the page from reading the response, because `*` is not allowed with credentials
Ignores the credentials option and silently retries the request without any cookies
Sends no request at all, because both origins share the parent domain `example.com`

questions.explanation: For credentialed requests, the browser rejects a wildcard `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. The server must echo the exact allowed origin (and send `Vary: Origin` if it varies), along with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. Echoing any origin blindly would let any site read users' authenticated data, so check it against an allowlist.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “Blocks the page from reading the response, because `*` is not allowed with credentials”. For credentialed requests, the browser rejects a wildcard `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`.
rubric: States the browser blocks the response.
Explains wildcard is forbidden with credentials.
Proposes echoing an allowlisted origin with Vary: Origin.
misconceptions: `*` allows everything, including cookies.
CORS stops the request from reaching the server.
